sections.h2: What should a seller know about Gainesville as a place?
sections.html:
Gainesville is Alachua County's seat and biggest city, and the city's own profile calls it the hub for work, school and shopping across the north central part of the state. It covers about 65.27 square miles, and the city's 2025 population figure is 151,275, based on University of Florida BEBR data.

The same profile gives a median age of 26.4 and median household income of $43,783 (2023 Census figures), numbers shaped by a big student presence at the University of Florida and Santa Fe College. Gainesville sits on the I-75 corridor, roughly halfway between Atlanta and Miami. It describes mild winters and warm summers, with a typical January high of 65 F, a June high of 89 F and around 35 inches of rain a year. A seller in a student-heavy area should expect a mix of owner-occupants and investors in the buyer pool.

sections.h2: Who bills a Gainesville property tax bill?
sections.html:
Alachua County bills it. Value and exemptions belong to the county's property appraiser, mailing and collection belong to its tax collector, and the city is only one of several bodies whose rates show up on the bill.

  • Tax collector: phone (352) 374-5236 if no bill arrives in November. Delinquent-tax payment questions go to its Tax Operations Department at (352) 264-6968.
  • Property appraiser: prepares the tax roll and decides homestead, disability, widow and agricultural exemptions. Its tangible division answers at (352) 374-5234.
  • City commission: sets the city millage as part of its annual budget.
  • County commission: sets county millage and certain non-ad valorem assessments.

Non-ad valorem charges on the bill include mandatory refuse collection, rural collection center, solid waste management, paving, water extension, fire, storm water and PACE assessments, according to the tax collector. Lower-income owners may be exempted from some of them through the county social services office at (352) 264-6750.

sections.h2: What is the City of Gainesville millage rate?
sections.html:
The city's facts page lists a millage rate of 6.7297 for fiscal year 2027, which means $6.7297 per $1,000 of taxable value. The city's final millage analysis, labeled as a staff recommendation, shows 6.7297 as the final and current rate, with a rolled-back rate of 6.3839 and a two-thirds vote maximum of 7.0223.

The same analysis says the figures are estimates until the Alachua County Property Appraiser's TRIM notice and the September hearings finalize them, and it gives a certified taxable value of $12,625,373,917 as of July 1, 2026. The city budget page also reports a 6.24 percent rise in taxable property values. Expect other lines on the same parcel from the county, the school board and the water district, so the city number alone does not give the total. Read the final rates on your November bill or ask the tax collector.

sections.h2: When are Alachua County taxes due and what is the discount?
sections.html:
Statements normally go out by the first of November. Full payment is due through March 31, and April 1 starts delinquency. The collector's discounts shrink month by month.

Alachua County discount by month paid
Month paidDiscount
November4%
December3%
January2%
February1%
MarchNone

Source: the Alachua County Tax Collector's property tax page. With a mortgage escrow account, the lender asks for the bill and you receive a copy for information only. The lender has to pay inside the 4 percent window. After a payoff, the lender must drop your account from its list, so a seller who just cleared a mortgage should confirm the bill now reaches them.

sections.h2: Can I pay Gainesville property tax in installments?
sections.html:
Yes, the county tax collector runs a four-payment plan for accounts whose prior-year tax tops $100. The sign-up cutoff is April 30 each year, and the 2026 cutoff has passed.

  • June 30: first payment, with a 6 percent reduction.
  • September 30: second payment, 4.5 percent reduction.
  • December 31: third payment, 3 percent reduction.
  • March 31: final payment at full price.

The opening pair each equal a quarter of last year's tax, and the closing pair divide what is left of the real liability. Skip the June payment and you drop out for the year, with a normal November bill to follow. A due date on a weekend or holiday slides to the next business day.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Gainesville property tax?
sections.html:
April 1 brings a 3 percent minimum charge on real estate tax, and the collector adds advertising costs in May after listing each late parcel in a local paper for three weeks. The online certificate sale runs through lienhub.com on or before June 1.

Bidders compete downward from an 18 percent rate. A certificate pays its holder at least 5 percent unless the winning bid is zero, and it is a first lien good for seven years. Once two years pass from delinquency, the holder may request a tax deed and the parcel heads to public auction. Paying the collector clears the lien.

For late tax the office takes cash, checks, money orders, debit cards (minimum $2.50 fee), e-check ($1.00) and credit cards or PayPal (2.5 percent fee). The date the office receives the payment sets the amount.

sections.h2: What if I own rental equipment or a business in Gainesville?
sections.html:
Tangible personal property tax covers furniture, fixtures and equipment in businesses or rentals, plus structural additions to mobile homes. The Alachua County Property Appraiser values it each January 1 from a return the owner files. Returns filed between January 1 and April 1 earn an exemption of up to $25,000, and late or missing returns bring penalties and lose it.

Unpaid personal property tax is late on April 1, when a $10 fee and 1.5 percent monthly interest begin. On May 1 the collector adds a collection fee of 20 percent of the gross tax, and a warrant adds a $50 legal fee. Questions go to the tangible division at (352) 374-5234.

sections.h2: How do homestead and deferral affect a Gainesville sale?
sections.html:
The city lists a homestead exemption of up to $50,000. The filing deadline is March 1 with the property appraiser, and the state's guide limits the home to your permanent residence. A statutory cap on assessed value growth, shown as 2.7 percent for 2026 on the state chart, protects owners, though a sale resets the next owner to just value.

The tax collector also describes a deferral. It is secured by a lien, carries interest capped at 7 percent a year, requires that the primary mortgage not exceed 70 percent of assessed value, and calls for insurance proof. A change of ownership makes the whole deferred amount payable, so the closing agent must pay it.

sections.h2: What should I do about tax before I sell in Gainesville?
sections.html:
Order a payoff from the Alachua County Tax Collector and add any deferral balance. The closing agent pays from proceeds. The collector adds that tangible tax on a business or rental is prorated between buyer and seller at closing, and a lien for that tax survives a sale, so owners of rentals should confirm no personal property bill is open.

Because the tax year runs January to December and the bill arrives in November, a closing in spring may still involve a bill the seller must settle. Cash buyers often meet short timelines, which helps ahead of an April 1 delinquency.

faqs.q: What is the Gainesville millage rate?
faqs.a: The city's facts page lists 6.7297 for fiscal year 2027, but the city's final analysis calls it a staff recommendation. Check the final rate on your bill or with the Alachua County Tax Collector.
The Alachua County Tax Collector. If you do not get a November bill, call (352) 374-5236.

faqs.q: When is Alachua County property tax late?
faqs.a: After March 31. Taxes become delinquent April 1, and a 3 percent minimum charge is added.

faqs.q: Is the Gainesville installment plan still open?
faqs.a: The 2026 application deadline of April 30 has passed. The plan returns every year, with sign-up by April 30 and a first payment by June 30.

faqs.q: Does a sale end my homestead deferral?
faqs.a: The deferral becomes due, with interest, when ownership changes. The closing agent should pay the balance from your proceeds.
